analysis.one_liner: Bars federal officials and their families from issuing, endorsing, or profiting from cryptocurrencies and stablecoins.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on June 23, 2025 and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it has received no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The COIN Act would stop covered federal officials — and their spouses, parents, children, and siblings — from issuing, sponsoring, or endorsing cryptocurrencies, meme coins, NFTs, and payment stablecoins while in office, and for 180 days before and 2 years after their term. It attaches fines and profit disgorgement, adds criminal penalties of up to 15 years when the conduct involves bribery or securities fraud, requires officials to disclose digital-asset holdings above $1,000, and forces approved stablecoin issuers to certify to the Office of Government Ethics that no public official profits from their coins [S2]. The bill was introduced by Senator Schiff with 10 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on June 23, 2025, where no further action has been taken [S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the public benefits from clearer rules against officeholders enriching themselves through digital-asset schemes — a niche where officials (or their families) launching or endorsing coins can cost ordinary retail investors, who often buy in based on the official's name or likeness. Rank-and-file retail investors are the most direct protected group, and honest officials benefit from a bright-line rule that removes pressure to monetize their office. The bill explicitly excludes ordinary purchase, sale, and holding of assets available to the general public, so it restrains official self-dealing, not routine investing [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and retail crypto investors

how_it_helps.text: It bans covered officials and their immediate family members from issuing, sponsoring, or endorsing cryptocurrencies, meme coins, tokens, NFTs, digital-asset securities and commodities, and payment stablecoins — including through derivatives or fund-based workarounds — during their term, the 180 days before it, and the two years after it [S2].

Violators face civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, 10% of the value of the interest, or the amount of their gain (whichever is greater), plus disgorgement of profits to the Treasury; knowing violations causing $1 million in losses to others, or tied to bribery or securities fraud, carry prison terms of up to 5 to 15 years and possible disqualification from federal office [S2].

It closes a loophole in existing federal conflict-of-interest law by declaring that a "financial interest" under 18 U.S.C. 208 includes interests in cryptocurrency and digital assets, so ordinary conflict rules clearly apply to them [S2].
It requires officials to disclose holdings of cryptocurrencies, meme coins, tokens, NFTs, and stablecoins worth more than $1,000 on their annual financial disclosures [S2].

It requires approved payment stablecoin issuers to certify to the Office of Government Ethics and their federal regulator that no public official profits from their stablecoin issuance, with the certifications published online and approval revoked if they fail to certify [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered officials and their immediate family members who would otherwise launch, sponsor, or endorse digital-asset ventures, and payment stablecoin issuers, who would bear recurring certification obligations and risk losing their regulatory approval to operate if they fail to certify [S2]. The Justice Department and Office of Government Ethics would take on new enforcement and publication duties [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Officials with crypto ventures and stablecoin issuers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not stop officials from personally buying, selling, or holding digital assets that are "routinely accessible to any member of the public" — the ban covers issuing, sponsoring, and endorsing, not trading — so unlike a full stock-trading ban it leaves most personal crypto investing untouched [S2].

Enforcement runs entirely through the Attorney General: only the Justice Department can bring the civil action for penalties and disgorgement, so if the Justice Department declines to act, the prohibition has no independent enforcer [S2].

The ban on fund-based exposure applies only where digital assets make up a "significant portion" of a mutual fund or ETF, with that threshold left to the Treasury Secretary to determine, creating regulatory uncertainty [S2].

Payment stablecoin issuers must submit certifications to the Office of Government Ethics and their regulator — initially, 90 days after first issuance, and quarterly thereafter — and can lose their approval to operate if they fail to certify, a recurring compliance cost [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: it closes a brand-new avenue for officeholders to cash in on public trust, in the exact niche (meme coins, celebrity tokens, stablecoins) where retail investors have been hurt, and it does not touch ordinary investing that any member of the public can do [S2]. The honest costs are modest: stablecoin issuers take on quarterly certification paperwork and risk losing their operating approval over a certification failure [S2]. The design's weak points are that it still lets officials trade crypto like anyone else, that all enforcement runs through one official (the Attorney General) who may simply decline to act, and that a key threshold ("significant portion" of a fund) is left to future Treasury determination [S2]. A stronger bill would also ban officials from trading digital assets and add independent enforcement; as written, this is a well-aimed but enforcement-dependent fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles government ethics, and no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 23, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S4].
The action history ends there: as of the latest record, the committee has not scheduled a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4].
Support is entirely Democratic: Senator Schiff introduced the bill with 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet — the bill is simply sitting in committee. If it stays there, the practical beneficiaries of the status quo are officeholders and crypto ventures, which face no new limits on official involvement in digital-asset deals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo preserved

for.name: Sen. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COIN Act on June 23, 2025, barring officials and their families from issuing, sponsoring, or endorsing digital assets, with civil and criminal penalties [S2].

for.name: Sens. Blunt Rochester, Cortez Masto, Gallego, Gillibrand, Luján, Slotkin, Kim, Blumenthal, and Alsobrooks
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill 11 Democratic Senate backers [S3].

sides.party_line_note: All 11 senators attached to the bill are Democrats [S3]; no Republican has cosponsored, and the record shows no Republican action for or against the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Cryptocurrency and digital-asset issuers (including payment stablecoin issuers)
industries.note: They can no longer put an official's name or likeness in marketing for a coin or token, and stablecoin issuers must certify quarterly that no public official profits from their issuance — and lose their approval to operate if they fail [S2]. Their interest in marketing through government figures runs against the public's interest in officials not cashing in on office.

industries.industry: Incumbent federal officeholders and their immediate families (concentrated interest of officials)
industries.note: They lose the ability to launch, sponsor, or endorse digital assets while in office, for 180 days before and two years after, with civil penalties and profit disgorgement, and criminal exposure of up to 15 years when violations involve bribery or securities fraud [S2]. This is the group the bill exists to restrain, and its interest in keeping that option open is directly opposed to the public's.

industries.industry: Mutual fund and ETF managers with digital-asset products
industries.note: Funds where digital assets make up a "significant portion" (as determined by Treasury) would be off-limits to officials and their families, a modest constraint with an undefined threshold [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee with no hearing or markup on record [S4]. Ethics and disclosure bills of this kind rarely reach the floor without committee action and a bipartisan cosponsor bloc, which this bill lacks. Absent a major scandal or a push from Senate leadership, the most likely path is that it remains in committee and dies when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, though it could be reintroduced in a future Congress.
